title: FlexTry-On: A Time-Efficient Framework for Multi-Scenario Virtual Try-on

paper.title: FlexTry-On: A Time-Efficient Framework for Multi-Scenario Virtual Try-on
paper.abstract: Abstract Virtual try-on has achieved remarkable progress in recent years, yet most existing methods are designed for a specific scenario, such as cloth-to-person or person-to-person try-on, and often require separate conditioning strategies and processing pipelines for different settings. We present FlexTry-On, a unified and time-efficient diffusion-based framework for diverse virtual try-on scenarios, including cloth-to-person, person-to-person, cross-domain, and in-the-wild settings. FlexTry-On adopts a common conditioning formulation, where a text-aware condition extraction strategy converts heterogeneous garment sources into a unified representation, and a dual-conditioning diffusion transformer jointly models garment appearance and person identity. Extensive experiments demonstrate competitive performance on both cloth-to-person and person-to-person benchmarks while maintaining fast inference. Moreover, the same framework can be directly applied to unseen cross-domain scenarios without requiring separate architectures or scenario-specific processing pipelines. These results highlight the potential of unified and efficient virtual try-on frameworks as a practical step toward more flexible and widely applicable virtual try-on systems.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Image-based virtual try-on (IVTON) aims to synthesize realistic images of a target person wearing a desired garment while preserving both garment appearance and human identity [ 5 ] . Recent advances in diffusion models [ 18 ] have significantly improved virtual try-on quality, leading to highly realistic results on standard benchmarks [ 32 , 3 , 8 , 19 , 23 ] . However, most existing methods are developed for a specific setting, such as cloth-to-person (C2P) or person-to-person (P2P) virtual try-on. In practice, garments may originate from clean product images, reference persons, or unconstrained real-world photographs. Existing virtual try-on systems, however, are typically tailored to a particular input format and scenario. Extending them to cross-domain or in-the-wild settings often requires additional assumptions, preprocessing steps, or task-specific adaptations, which also introduce additional computational overhead. As a result, virtual try-on remains fragmented across scenarios despite sharing the same underlying objective of garment transfer. A key challenge is how to convert garments from heterogeneous sources into a unified conditioning representation while preserving garment appearance and person identity. Can a single virtual try-on framework effectively handle diverse virtual try-on scenarios? In this paper, we present FlexTry-On , a unified and time-efficient diffusion-based framework for cloth-to-person, person-to-person, cross-domain, and in-the-wild virtual try-on. To accommodate heterogeneous garment sources, FlexTry-On first employs a Text-Aware Segmentation Module (TASM) that extracts task-aware garment conditions from either product images or reference persons. These conditions are converted into a unified conditioning representation and processed by a Dual-DiT Tryon Module (DDTM), where a reference branch captures garment appearance and a try-on branch synthesizes the final image while preserving person identity. In addition, we employ a Style-GRAM loss to encourage appearance consistency between the generated garment region and the reference garment, improving garment preservation under noisy supervision. Together, these components enable the same framework to support diverse virtual try-on scenarios through a shared conditioning and generation pipeline. By formulating diverse virtual try-on tasks under a common conditional generation framework, FlexTry-On eliminates the need for scenario-specific architectures and maintains a consistent inference pipeline across different settings. Furthermore, the same framework supports multiple garment categories within a unified conditioning formulation, enabling a unified formulation across different virtual try-on scenarios. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FlexTry-On achieves competitive visual quality and strong FID [ 17 ] performance on both C2P and P2P benchmarks while maintaining efficient inference. In addition, the same framework can be directly applied to challenging cross-domain and in-the-wild scenarios. As shown in Fig. 2 , FlexTry-On achieves a favorable balance between synthesis quality, inference efficiency, and scenario flexibility, providing a practical step toward more flexible and widely applicable virtual try-on systems. Our contributions are summarized as: 1. We propose FlexTry-On, a unified and time-efficient diffusion-based framework that bridges cloth-to-person, person-to-person, cross-domain, and in-the-wild virtual try-on scenarios within a single framework. 2. We introduce a unified virtual try-on framework consisting of a Text-Aware Segmentation Module (TASM) and a Dual-DiT Tryon Module (DDTM), enabling conditioning from heterogeneous garment sources while jointly modeling garment appearance and person identity. We further employ a Style-GRAM loss for garment appearance preservation under noisy supervision. 3. Extensive evaluations on both standard benchmarks and challenging real-world settings demonstrate competitive visual quality, strong FID performance, and efficient inference within a unified framework. sections.heading: 2 Related Works
sections.text: IVTON [ 5 ] has evolved from warping-based pipelines to diffusion-based generative frameworks. Early methods [ 16 , 36 , 41 , 2 , 25 , 8 ] rely on explicit garment alignment and image synthesis, making them sensitive to pose variations, occlusions, and inaccurate geometric estimation. Recent diffusion-based approaches [ 49 , 32 , 13 , 22 , 3 , 45 , 4 , 23 , 15 , 26 , 29 ] significantly improve visual quality through large pre-trained models and attention-based mechanisms. Despite these advances, most existing methods are designed around specific conditioning assumptions. Many diffusion-based IVTON approaches assume a particular garment representation, such as clean product images, extracted garment regions, or reference-person-based garment cues, and design their conditioning mechanisms accordingly [ 49 , 32 , 13 , 22 , 3 , 45 , 4 , 23 , 15 , 26 , 29 ] . Consequently, their conditioning mechanisms are often tailored to specific input formats, limiting both flexibility and efficiency across different virtual try-on scenarios. Furthermore, most existing methods [ 49 , 32 , 13 , 22 , 3 , 45 , 4 , 23 , 26 , 29 ] implicitly assume category-consistent garment transfer, where the source and target garments belong to the same clothing category (e.g., upper-to-upper or dress-to-dress). Under this assumption, editable regions can be determined using predefined masks, human parsing labels, or garment extraction pipelines. However, transfers across different garment categories introduce ambiguous editable regions that cannot be uniquely determined using conventional category-based masking strategies. Recent methods, including Mask Does Not Matter [ 9 ] , All Parts Matter [ 10 ] , OmniTry [ 11 ] , OmniVTON [ 44 ] , and M&M VTO [ 48 ] , extend virtual try-on beyond the conventional cloth-to-person setting toward more diverse and realistic applications. Nevertheless, they are primarily designed for specific input assumptions and do not explicitly address category-crossing transfers. These observations suggest the key challenge is not only generating realistic try-on images but also designing a framework that can accommodate heterogeneous garment sources, identify task-aware editable regions, and support diverse virtual try-on scenarios without sacrificing inference efficiency. sections.heading: 3 Methodology
sections.text: To support diverse virtual try-on scenarios within a single framework, we propose FlexTry-On, a diffusion-based approach that accommodates different input modalities and garment categories under a unified formulation. FlexTry-On consists of two key components: a Text-Aware Segmentation Module (TASM), which converts heterogeneous garment inputs into task-aware garment conditions and editable regions, and a Dual-DiT TryOn Module (DDTM), which synthesizes the final try-on image by jointly modeling garment appearance and person identity. Built on a DiT-based latent diffusion framework [ 39 , 35 ] , FlexTry-On encodes inputs into a shared latent space using a pre-trained VAE. DDTM employs a dual-DiT design, where a reference DiT extracts garment representations only once and a try-on DiT performs image synthesis through denoising. This design enables a unified and computationally efficient pipeline for cloth-to-person, person-to-person, and cross-domain virtual try-on scenarios. Figure 4 : Overview of the Dual-DiT Tryon Module (DDTM). The DDTM follows a DiT-based architecture [ 35 ] with cross-attention to integrate person and garment information. During training, different conditioning strategies are adopted for C2P and P2P settings. For clarity, patchification and positional embeddings are omitted.

sections.heading: 3.1 Text-Aware Segmentation Module (TASM)
sections.text: To support diverse virtual try-on scenarios, we introduce a Text-Aware Segmentation Module (TASM) that converts heterogeneous inputs into a unified conditioning representation. Unlike conventional human parsing models [ 28 ] or generic segmentation frameworks such as SAM [ 24 ] and Grounded-SAM [ 30 , 37 ] that are designed for pixel-level segmentation, TASM is designed specifically for virtual try-on conditioning and operates directly in the latent space. Given an image and predefined text conditions, TASM predicts garment-specific masks for downstream conditioning. As illustrated in Fig. 3 , TASM adopts a DiT-based architecture [ 35 ] and injects text conditions through multi-head cross-attention. Given a latent image representation, the module predicts region-specific masks corresponding to different garment categories. Specifically, only the predicted masks are retained for subsequent processing, while associated latent appearance features are discarded. An ablation of this design is provided in Appendix A.1 . The objective function is a combination of reconstruction ℒ 1 , ℒ 2 \mathcal{L}_{1},\mathcal{L}_{2} and adversarial objectives: ℒ textseg = ℒ 1 + ℒ 2 + α GAN ​ ℒ GAN , \mathcal{L}_{\text{textseg}}=\mathcal{L}_{1}+\mathcal{L}_{2}+\alpha_{\text{GAN}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{GAN}}, (1) where α GAN \alpha_{\text{GAN}} controls the contribution of the adversarial loss [ 20 ] . Ground-truth masks follow the protocol of [ 47 ] , supplemented with additional annotations for facial, hair, and accessory regions from [ 28 ] . To construct the garment-agnostic mask used in the try-on stage, TASM predicts region-specific masks according to predefined text conditions. These masks are merged as: M g ​ a = RECT ⁡ [ M i ​ c ∨ M i ​ s ​ k ] ∖ M i ​ f ​ h , M_{ga}=\mathrm{RECT}\left[M_{ic}\lor M_{isk}\right]\setminus M_{ifh}, (2) where M i ​ c M_{ic} , M i ​ s ​ k M_{isk} , and M i ​ f ​ h M_{ifh} denote the clothing, skin, and face-with-hands masks, respectively, and RECT ⁡ [ ⋅ ] \mathrm{RECT}[\cdot] represents the enclosing rectangular region. This formulation enables flexible region control across cross-domain try-on settings (e.g., dress-to-upper or upper–lower-to-dress), as illustrated in Fig. 6 . Unlike conventional human parsing [ 28 , 21 ] , TASM generates task-specific masks that explicitly identify the regions involved in the try-on process. By decoupling editable-region construction from predefined garment categories, TASM directly supports cross-domain virtual try-on scenarios where conventional category-dependent masking strategies become ambiguous. Additional discussion is provided in Appendix G.1 .

sections.heading: 3.2 Dual-DiT Tryon Module (DDTM)
sections.text: The Dual-DiT Tryon Module consists of two diffusion transformer branches [ 35 ] : a Reference Net and a Main Net, as illustrated in Fig. 4 . The Reference Net extracts garment-related features, while the Main Net performs try-on synthesis. This dual-stream design decouples garment appearance modeling from the generation process, providing structured guidance throughout denoising. Given a garment image I g I_{g} and a person image I p I_{p} , TASM constructs the garment condition z g = ℰ ⁡ ( I g ) ⊙ M g z_{g}=\mathcal{E}(I_{g})\odot M_{g} , where M g M_{g} denotes the garment mask. Similarly, the garment-agnostic person condition is constructed as z g ​ a = ℰ ⁡ ( I p ) ⊙ M g ​ a z_{ga}=\mathcal{E}(I_{p})\odot M_{ga} , where M g ​ a M_{ga} is predicted by TASM. For P2P, TASM extracts M g M_{g} from the reference person to isolate the source garment, whereas for C2P the clean product garment is directly retained. Thus, the same interface accommodates both product-garment and person-reference inputs. The Reference Net processes z g z_{g} once at a fixed diffusion timestep [ 3 ] , producing multi-level garment features that are reused throughout denoising. The Main Net receives the noisy latent z t z_{t} , garment-agnostic latent z g ​ a z_{ga} , mask M g ​ a M_{ga} , pose keypoints ℰ ⁡ ( J p ) \mathcal{E}(J_{p}) , and DensePose map ℰ ⁡ ( I d ​ p ) \mathcal{E}(I_{dp}) . These spatial conditions are patch-embedded and concatenated to form the global conditioning input. Intermediate Reference-Net features are combined with garment-type text embeddings and injected into the corresponding Main-Net layers through cross-attention. This design provides multi-level garment guidance while separating garment feature extraction from iterative image synthesis.

sections.heading: 3.2.2 GRAM-based Style Objective
sections.text: A fundamental requirement of IVTON is that the target garment must appear in the final synthesized result. However, the diffusion denoising objective primarily supervises image reconstruction and does not explicitly optimize garment fidelity, particularly on large-scale datasets with noisy garment-person correspondences [ 40 ] . Specifically, samples may share the same garment category while differing substantially in color, texture, or fine-grained appearance. Under such conditions, the model can satisfy the denoising objective while gradually reducing its reliance on garment-specific cues, leading to degraded garment fidelity. An illustrative mis-pairing example is provided in Fig. 5 . To bridge this gap, we introduce a GRAM-based Style Loss as a task-alignment constraint that explicitly encourages preservation of garment-specific appearance cues. Although GRAM-based style losses are not new [ 12 ] , our contribution lies in revisiting them as an optimization objective for virtual try-on rather than image stylization. Unlike pixel-wise reconstruction losses, which are incompatible with the geometric variations inherent in virtual try-on, the proposed loss operates on appearance statistics and remains invariant to spatial layout, making it particularly effective for preserving garment color and texture during synthesis. The style loss is defined as: ℒ s ​ t ​ y ​ l ​ e = MSE ⁡ ( G ⁡ ( z g ) , G ⁡ ( z o ​ u ​ t ⊙ M i ​ c ) ) , \mathcal{L}_{style}=\mathrm{MSE}\Big(G(z_{g}),\,G(z_{out}\odot M_{ic})\Big), (4) where G ⁡ ( ⋅ ) G(\cdot) denotes the Gram matrix, z g z_{g} represents the latent garment condition, and z o ​ u ​ t ⊙ M i ​ c z_{out}\odot M_{ic} extracts the predicted garment region from the denoised latent. This loss explicitly enforces the diffusion model to preserve garment-related appearance statistics throughout the synthesis process, ensuring that the generated output remains consistent with the reference garment in terms of color and texture. Unlike reconstruction-oriented objectives used in prior work [ 38 , 7 ] , the proposed GRAM-based loss does not aim to recover exact pixel values; instead, it serves as a task-aligned constraint that directly reflects the essential requirement of IVTON. As discussed in Sec. 4.3.2 , this design improves garment appearance preservation under both curated and noisy training, with substantially larger gains under noisy supervision, and helps maintain garment appearance under pose and identity variations. The total loss is formulated as: ℒ t ​ o ​ t ​ a ​ l = ℒ d ​ e ​ n ​ o ​ i ​ s ​ e + α s ​ t ​ y ​ l ​ e ​ ℒ s ​ t ​ y ​ l ​ e , \mathcal{L}_{total}=\mathcal{L}_{denoise}+\alpha_{style}\mathcal{L}_{style}, (5) where α s ​ t ​ y ​ l ​ e \alpha_{style} is the balance coefficient for the style loss. sections.heading: 4.2.1 Baseline Comparison
sections.text: Tab. 1 compares FlexTry-On with prior diffusion-based IVTON methods. Publicly released checkpoints are used whenever available. For runtime evaluation, FlexTry-On uses 30 denoising steps, whereas each baseline follows its default inference configuration. All directly reproducible methods are measured with batch size 1 on a single RTX 4090 (24GB VRAM); exceptions and hardware normalization are detailed in Appendix E . All evaluations are conducted at 512 × 512 512\times 512 resolution. For methods without official implementations, we report paper-reported results. For OmniVTON [ 44 ] , we attempted to reproduce the official implementation but encountered unresolved issues and therefore retain its published quantitative results. FlexTry-On achieves the best paired/unpaired FID on both VITON-HD and DressCode-Upper among the evaluated methods while maintaining fast inference. Its efficiency comes from a single Reference-Net pass for garment feature extraction, followed by iterative denoising in the Main Net, avoiding repeated garment-side computation across denoising steps. Qualitative results in Fig. 7 further show more consistent garment texture and structure preservation, with fewer arm-region artifacts and clothing inconsistencies.

sections.heading: 4.2.2 Full Dataset Training
sections.text: To support multiple IVTON scenarios within a single model, we train FlexTry-On* on the full combined C2P–P2P corpus. As shown in Tab. 1 , FlexTry-On* supports C2P, P2P, and cross-domain C2P/P2P, providing broader scenario coverage than the compared methods. We evaluate its standard C2P performance on the VITON-HD [ 2 ] and DressCode [ 33 ] Upper test sets. Compared with FlexTry-On trained only on VITON-HD and DressCode, FlexTry-On* shows a modest reduction in standard C2P performance (5.51/8.97 vs. 6.34/9.22 paired/unpaired FID on VITON-HD) , while enabling P2P and cross-domain scenarios within the same model. This illustrates the trade-off between optimizing for a single benchmark setting and supporting broader scenarios. As shown in Fig. 8 , FlexTry-On* supports P2P in both same-domain and zero-shot cross-domain settings. We further compare it with CatVTON and ITA-MDT*, a retrained variant of ITA-MDT. For cross-domain dress transfer, these methods require manually defined full-garment masks to specify the editable region because their original masking strategies are designed for category-consistent try-on. Even with these manually adapted masks, preserving garment structure and appearance across categories remains challenging. Meanwhile, TASM automatically constructs task-aware editable regions, allowing FlexTry-On* to produce more coherent results with better garment texture and structure preservation. Additional cross-domain examples, including dress-to-lower, dress-to-upper, and upper-lower-to-dress transfers in C2P/P2P, are provided in Appendix C . sections.heading: 4.2.3 In-the-wild Evaluation
sections.text: On Street Try-On [ 6 ] , both FlexTry-On and OmniVTON are evaluated zero-shot, without training on StreetTryOn. As shown in Tab. 3 , FlexTry-On performs better on Shop2Street and Model2Street, whereas the paper-reported OmniVTON results are better on Model2Model and Street2Street. Street2Street remains challenging due to uncontrolled pose, illumination, background, and occlusion, especially when the source garment is small or partially visible (Appendix H). For OmniVTON [ 44 ] , we retain the published StreetTryOn scores for comparison. However, our evaluation using the official repository did not reproduce the reported performance and produced degraded outputs (Fig. 9 ). This discrepancy suggests that the results may depend on implementation details or evaluation conditions not captured by the released setup. Thus, these results are paper-reported rather than independently verified, and the reported inference times are not directly comparable across environments. sections.heading: 4.3.1 Effectiveness of TASM
sections.text: We compare TASM with conventional human parsing and Grounded-SAM (G-SAM) [ 30 , 37 ] . Because reliable ground-truth masks are unavailable, particularly for cross-domain cases, and mask accuracy does not directly measure conditioning quality, we evaluate downstream try-on performance rather than Boundary IoU [ 1 ] . Replacing TASM degrades quantitative and visual quality (Tab. 2 , Fig. 10 (A)(D)), producing incomplete garment preservation and retained body regions. Although trained from G-SAM pseudo-labels, TASM provides better task-aware conditioning than G-SAM. Its latent-space design also supports category-aware cross-domain masking without additional supervision; pixel-space alternatives are discussed in Sec. A.2 .

sections.heading: 4.3.3 Effect of Extended Training Data on Prior Methods
sections.text: To separate model design from data scale, we retrain StableVITON, CAT-DM, and ITA-MDT on the same C2P–P2P corpus, adapting their released checkpoints with segmented person garments while following the original protocols. Methods requiring additional conditioning are excluded. Tab. 4 and Fig. 11 evaluate the resulting checkpoints in both settings. With matched training data, FlexTry-On achieves the best paired/unpaired FID in both C2P and P2P.Qualitative results in Fig. 11 further support this result, showing more consistent garment appearance and fewer distortions under pose and identity changes. Taken together, these controlled comparisons indicate that the observed gains cannot be explained by the broader training corpus alone, but also reflect the effectiveness of the proposed unified conditioning and generation framework.

sections.heading: 5 Limitations
sections.text: FlexTry-On remains challenged by severe occlusion, unusual or oversized garments, and Street-to-Street cases involving uncontrolled pose, illumination, background, and occlusion. The current pipeline assumes a single selected visible person and does not automatically handle crowded or multi-person scenes. The combined training corpus may also inherit demographic and social-media biases. In addition, FlexTry-On does not consistently outperform all baselines on SSIM/LPIPS, despite achieving stronger FID in several settings. The OmniVTON comparison relies on paper-reported quantitative results because our local reproduction was unsuccessful. Additional discussion and failure analysis are provided in Appendices G and H . The full training corpus also contains weakly aligned garment–person pairs; ℒ s ​ t ​ y ​ l ​ e \mathcal{L}_{style} mitigates their effect on garment preservation but does not eliminate supervision noise. In practice, FlexTry-On targets single-person try-on applications where a target person and garment are specified before inference; automatic person selection in crowded scenes is outside the current scope.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We present FlexTry-On, a unified framework for C2P, P2P, cross-domain, and in-the-wild virtual try-on. TASM provides task-aware editable regions, DDTM enables efficient synthesis with a single garment-reference pass, and ℒ s ​ t ​ y ​ l ​ e \mathcal{L}_{style} improves garment preservation under noisy supervision. FlexTry-On achieves competitive quality with 1.2-s inference, while matched retraining and qualitative results support its effectiveness across diverse try-on settings.

sections.heading: A.1 Empirical Justification of the TASM Design
sections.text: This ablation investigates a key design choice of TASM. Although TASM predicts both latent appearance representations and segmentation masks, only the masks are used during try-on inference. The latent representations serve solely as an auxiliary supervision signal during training, raising the question about this branch’s necessary. To answer this question, we construct a simplified variant, denoted as TASM-MaskOnly , which predicts segmentation masks only while retaining the same architecture and training objective. An overview of both designs is shown in Fig. A . As described in the main paper, TASM injects text conditions through multi-head cross-attention and scale-and-shift modulation. Both variants are integrated into the same Dual-DiT framework with the Style-GRAM loss, trained on VITON-HD and DressCode in the C2P setting and evaluated on their respective Upper test sets. We hypothesize that latent prediction acts as an auxiliary representation-learning task. While mask supervision mainly focuses on region boundaries, reconstructing latent garment representations requires the model to capture garment semantics, appearance, and spatial extent simultaneously. Consequently, the learned features become more informative for segmentation, potentially leading to more accurate mask prediction even though the latent outputs are discarded during inference. Quantitative results in Tab. A show that TASM consistently outperforms TASM-MaskOnly across nearly all metrics. Qualitative comparisons in Fig. B further reveal that TASM-MaskOnly frequently fails to accurately localize garment regions, particularly for lower-body garments, leading to degraded try-on results. These findings support our hypothesis that auxiliary latent prediction improves region understanding and contributes to higher-quality garment masks, despite not being used during inference.

sections.text: ”Why not light-weight pixel segmentation?” FastSAM, a lightweight SAM, is designed by sacrificing segmentation accuracy for speed relative to SAM. Our empirical advantage over the SAM-based approach further supports TASM’s effectiveness. These results motivate the latent-space formulation of TASM. By focusing on semantically consistent garment regions rather than exact contours, TASM improves robustness, computational efficiency, and compatibility with diffusion-based synthesis, while enabling more flexible scenarios such as cross-domain try-on. sections.heading: Appendix C Cross-Domain Qualitative Results
sections.text: This section presents additional qualitative results on cross-domain virtual try-on, where the garment category of the reference input differs from that of the target person. Such settings are particularly challenging because they violate the category-consistency assumption commonly adopted by existing virtual try-on methods. One representative scenario involves transferring a dress or full-body garment onto a person wearing separate upper and lower garments. As shown in Fig. G , FlexTry-On produces realistic results in both C2P and P2P settings while preserving fine-grained garment details, including complex patterns, transparency effects, and structural characteristics. A second scenario considers transferring upper or lower garments onto a person wearing a dress. This requires determining which regions should be preserved and which should participate in the try-on process. By leveraging text-aware garment masks, FlexTry-On can effectively handle these ambiguous boundaries and generate coherent results across different category transformations. Examples are shown in Fig. H , Fig. I , Fig. J , and Fig. K . In contrast, methods relying on conventional human parsing [ 28 ] do not natively define task-specific editable regions for cross-domain configurations, particularly dress-to-upper and dress-to-lower try-on. For visualization purposes, when evaluating ITA-MDT* and CatVTON in these settings, we manually mask all clothing regions on the input person to define the inpainting area. Even with this manually adapted masking strategy, FlexTry-On produces more coherent and visually consistent results. These examples demonstrate how the proposed unified framework extends beyond conventional C2P and P2P settings to challenging cross-domain virtual try-on scenarios.

sections.heading: Appendix D Text-aware Segmentation Module Training Configuration
sections.text: Figure B : Ablation study results on VITON-HD [ 2 ] to evaluate the effectiveness of the TASM module architecture design in the clean datasets. The DDTM denotes the Dual-DiT Tryon Module, which is trained only on the clean dataset (VITON-HD [ 2 ] and DressCode [ 33 ] ). In this section, we provide the handcrafted text conditions used to train TASM and discuss the rationale behind their design. Unlike conventional human parsing, which assigns each pixel to a fixed semantic category, TASM aims to produce task-oriented masks that can support diverse virtual try-on scenarios, including cross-domain settings. Therefore, the predefined text conditions are organized according to functional garment regions rather than dataset-specific semantic labels. The classes and corresponding text conditions are listed below: 1. Upper body Clothes: ’inner shirt or inner t-shirt or top, or bra’ 2. Lower body Clothes: ’shorts, or pants, or skirt, or trousers, or underwear’ 3. Full body Clothes: ’dresses, or jumpsuits, or overalls’ 4. Outer Clothes: ’jackets, or blazers, or outer shirt, or long padding jackets’ 5. Face and hand: ’face and hand’ 6. Shoes: ’shoes’ 7. Bag: ’bags’ 8. Upper Body Skin (neck and arms): ’upper body skin’ 9. Lower Body Skin (legs): ’lower body skin’ 10. Full Body Skin (neck, arms, and legs): ’full body skin’ The region-preservation strategy is designed according to the target garment category. Intuitively, regions unrelated to the target garment should be preserved whenever possible to maintain visual consistency. For example, during upper-body try-on, lower garments and lower-body skin are retained, whereas during lower-body try-on, upper garments and upper-body skin are preserved. For full-body and outerwear try-on, only identity-related and accessory regions, such as faces, hands, shoes, and bags, are retained. This design is particularly important for cross-domain virtual try-on. Consider the case of transferring an upper garment onto a person wearing a dress. Conventional human parsing typically treats the entire dress as a single semantic region, making it difficult to determine which parts should be preserved and which should participate in the try-on process. In contrast, the proposed text-conditioned decomposition enables TASM to generate task-specific masks, providing more flexible region control across diverse garment categories and cross-domain scenarios.

sections.heading: Appendix E Implementation Details
sections.text: This section provides additional implementation details of the proposed framework. For preprocessing, we use MediaPipe [ 34 ] for pose keypoint extraction and DensePose [ 14 ] for dense body correspondence estimation. The proposed Dual-DiT Tryon Module (DDTM) is built upon DiT-XL/2 [ 35 ] , with 28 transformer layers, including 4 decoding layers, a hidden dimension of 1152, and 16 attention heads. All images are resized to 512 × 512 512\times 512 . Following prior work, we employ the SD 2.0 VAE [ 39 ] , which encodes images into latent representations of size 64 × 64 × 4 64\times 64\times 4 . During training, we use 1000 diffusion timesteps and perform inference with 30 denoising steps. The model is optimized using a learning rate of 1 × 10 − 4 1\times 10^{-4} and an EMA decay of 0.9999. All remaining optimization settings, including the optimizer and learning-rate scheduler, follow the original DiT configuration [ 35 ] . The classifier-free guidance scale is set to 2.0. Unless otherwise specified, reported results correspond to the model trained for 1.5M iterations. Training is conducted on either 8 NVIDIA A6000 GPUs (48GB each) or 4 NVIDIA H200 GPUs (141GB each), depending on hardware availability. Within every ablation pair, the variants with and without ℒ s ​ t ​ y ​ l ​ e \mathcal{L}_{style} use the same batch size, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, and number of training iterations; only the loss term is changed. The Text-Aware Segmentation Module (TASM) is built upon DiT-B/2, consisting of 12 transformer layers, a hidden dimension of 768, and 12 attention heads. TASM is trained for 800K iterations on a single RTX 4090 GPU (24GB) with a batch size of 7. For inference-time measurement, all methods are benchmarked on an RTX 4090 GPU with 24GB memory whenever possible. Since OmniTry-On and Any2Any Try-On cannot be directly evaluated on this platform, we first measure their runtime on an RTX A6000 GPU with 48GB memory and estimate the corresponding RTX 4090 runtime using the runtime scaling factor of our method measured on both GPUs. The controlled module comparison reports online segmentation and denoising; pose, DensePose, and other preprocessing are identical across the compared variants and therefore excluded. For the G-SAM baseline [ 30 , 37 ] , we use GroundingDINO-Tiny followed by SAM-B with their publicly released checkpoints, without any additional fine-tuning. Runtime is measured for one batch-size-1 try-on. Each segmentation method must evaluate all 10 segmentation-class conditions listed above for the same input image. TASM evaluates these conditions together as one batch in 0.1 s. In contrast, the GroundingDINO–SAM pipeline processes the 10 class conditions sequentially, requiring approximately 1.9 s per class, or 19.0 s per try-on. sections.heading: Appendix F Dataset and Evaluation
sections.text: This section describes the datasets used for training and evaluation. To support diverse virtual try-on scenarios, we construct a unified training corpus from VITON-HD [ 2 ] , DressCode [ 33 ] , DeepFashion [ 31 ] , IMAGDress [ 40 ] , and a filtered subset of LRVS-Fashion [ 27 ] . These datasets provide both C2P and P2P samples across diverse garment categories, poses, identities, and backgrounds. VITON-HD provides 11,647 training and 2,032 test images at 1024 × 768 1024\times 768 . DressCode contains over 50,000 images covering upper-body, lower-body, and dresses. DeepFashion contributes 52,712 images for P2P training. IMAGDress contains 324,857 paired samples, while approximately 500,000 downloadable LRVS-Fashion images are retained after filtering. All datasets are standardized into four garment categories, yielding approximately 930,000 training samples in total. Detailed statistics are reported in Tab. C . We report LPIPS [ 46 ] , SSIM [ 42 ] , and FID [ 17 ] . Lower LPIPS/FID and higher SSIM indicate better performance. To evaluate inference-seed sensitivity, we repeat inference on VITON-HD with seeds { 0 , 1 , 2 } \{0,1,2\} using the same checkpoint. Seed-wise paired/unpaired FID is reported in Tab. B (b). We report both paired and unpaired FID. Paired FID evaluates reconstruction against corresponding ground truth, whereas unpaired FID evaluates unseen garment–person combinations and serves as the primary metric for the standard unpaired IVTON setting.

sections.heading: G.1 Inpainting Mask Strategy
sections.text: In most prior IVTON methods, the inpainting mask is determined by the try-on garment category. For example, when the target garment is an upper-body item (e.g., a T-shirt or shirt), the mask is typically constructed from the corresponding upper-body garment region of the person together with exposed skin regions, while preserving the hands, face, and hair. A similar strategy is applied to lower-body garments. For full-body garments such as dresses, the editable region generally covers all clothing regions and relevant body areas while preserving identity-related regions such as the face, hair, and hands. However, such category-dependent masking becomes ambiguous in cross-domain try-on settings. For instance, when a person is wearing a dress, conventional human parsing does not directly determine which part of the dress should be edited when the target garment is an upper- or lower-body item. Consequently, existing category-based masking strategies cannot naturally define the corresponding editable region. TASM addresses this issue by producing task-aware, text-conditioned masks according to the target garment category. For qualitative comparison in dress-to-upper and dress-to-lower settings, we adapt prior methods by treating the editable clothing area as a full-body region, allowing them to generate outputs under their existing masking pipelines. The resulting comparisons are shown in Fig. 6 in the main paper and Figs. H , I , J , and K . Figure C : Representative Street2Street failure cases on Street Try-On [ 6 ] . sections.heading: G.3 Evaluation Scope and Reproducibility
sections.text: Our quantitative evaluation covers standard C2P benchmarks and matched-data C2P–P2P evaluation. Specifically, C2P is evaluated using paired and unpaired VITON-HD and DressCode protocols, while Tab. 4 compares methods retrained on the same C2P–P2P corpus. Because no standardized paired benchmark exists for the category-changing transitions considered in our cross-domain experiments, we restrict this capability to zero-shot qualitative evaluation. Paired metrics evaluate reconstruction against corresponding targets, whereas unpaired FID evaluates unseen garment–person combinations and remains the primary metric for standard unpaired IVTON. Using the same checkpoint, three inference seeds yield paired/unpaired FID standard deviations of 0.02/0.01, indicating low sensitivity to sampling randomness.

sections.heading: G.4 Efficiency and Computational Footprint
sections.text: The controlled TASM–G-SAM comparison isolates segmentation as the only differing component. TASM evaluates all 10 text conditions jointly in 0.1 s, whereas G-SAM processes them sequentially in approximately 19.0 s. Both are followed by the same 1.1 s DDTM inference. Shared pose and DensePose preprocessing is excluded from this controlled comparison. Precomputing G-SAM masks would remove this online segmentation cost, but would not affect the downstream conditioning-quality comparison in Tab. 2 . FlexTry-On contains 1.634B parameters across its three DiT modules and 2.058B parameters when including the frozen VAE and CLIP text encoder. At 512 × 512 512\times 512 resolution, batch size 1, and BF16 precision, inference requires 5.15 GB peak allocated GPU memory.

sections.heading: Appendix H Limitations
sections.text: Our framework is built upon an inpainting-based formulation and therefore inherits limitations common to diffusion-based virtual try-on methods. In particular, extremely oversized or unconventional garments remain challenging when their desired geometry extends substantially beyond the editable region. Performance may also degrade under severe occlusion or for highly complex garment structures that are underrepresented in the training data. Street-to-Street transfer is particularly challenging because both the source garment and target person may exhibit uncontrolled pose, illumination, background, garment appearance, and occlusion. Moreover, when the reference garment occupies only a small region of the source image, fine-grained garment cues become less informative, making garment-identity preservation more difficult and increasing the tendency to hallucinate garment details. Representative failure cases are shown in Fig. C . In these examples, FlexTry-On captures the overall garment appearance but may fail to faithfully preserve fine-grained details and geometry, such as patterns, necklines, sleeve shapes, and silhouettes. These failures are more pronounced when the reference garment is small or partially occluded, suggesting that limited garment evidence remains a key challenge in unconstrained Street-to-Street settings. The current preprocessing pipeline assumes that a single visible target person has been selected before inference. It does not automatically handle multiple people, person-to-person occlusion, or ambiguous target selection in crowded scenes. In addition, the combined training corpus inherits demographic and social-media collection biases; our current evaluation does not establish uniform performance across demographic groups. These limitations motivate future work on more robust garment representations under limited visual evidence, automatic multi-person target selection, and broader, demographically balanced virtual try-on datasets. We present FlexTry-On, a unified and time-efficient diffusion-based framework for diverse virtual try-on scenarios, including cloth-to-person, person-to-person, cross-domain, and in-the-wild settings. FlexTry-On adopts a common conditioning formulation, where a text-aware condition extraction strategy converts heterogeneous garment sources into a unified representation, and a dual-conditioning diffusion transformer jointly models garment appearance and person identity. Extensive experiments demonstrate competitive performance on both cloth-to-person and person-to-person benchmarks while maintaining fast inference. Moreover, the same framework can be directly applied to unseen cross-domain scenarios without requiring separate architectures or scenario-specific processing pipelines. These results highlight the potential of unified and efficient virtual try-on frameworks as a practical step toward more flexible and widely applicable virtual try-on systems. Please zoom in for a clearer visualization of fine details. 1 Introduction Image-based virtual try-on (IVTON) aims to synthesize realistic images of a target person wearing a desired garment while preserving both garment appearance and human identity [ 5 ] . Recent advances in diffusion models [ 18 ] have significantly improved virtual try-on quality, leading to highly realistic results on standard benchmarks [ 32 , 3 , 8 , 19 , 23 ] . However, most existing methods are developed for a specific setting, such as cloth-to-person (C2P) or person-to-person (P2P) virtual try-on. In practice, garments may originate from clean product images, reference persons, or unconstrained real-world photographs. Existing virtual try-on systems, however, are typically tailored to a particular input format and scenario. Extending them to cross-domain or in-the-wild settings often requires additional assumptions, preprocessing steps, or task-specific adaptations, which also introduce additional computational overhead. As a result, virtual try-on remains fragmented across scenarios despite sharing the same underlying objective of garment transfer. A key challenge is how to convert garments from heterogeneous sources into a unified conditioning representation while preserving garment appearance and person identity. Can a single virtual try-on framework effectively handle diverse virtual try-on scenarios? In this paper, we present FlexTry-On , a unified and time-efficient diffusion-based framework for cloth-to-person, person-to-person, cross-domain, and in-the-wild virtual try-on. To accommodate heterogeneous garment sources, FlexTry-On first employs a Text-Aware Segmentation Module (TASM) that extracts task-aware garment conditions from either product images or reference persons. These conditions are converted into a unified conditioning representation and processed by a Dual-DiT Tryon Module (DDTM), where a reference branch captures garment appearance and a try-on branch synthesizes the final image while preserving person identity. In addition, we employ a Style-GRAM loss to encourage appearance consistency between the generated garment region and the reference garment, improving garment preservation under noisy supervision. Together, these components enable the same framework to support diverse virtual try-on scenarios through a shared conditioning and generation pipeline. By formulating diverse virtual try-on tasks under a common conditional generation framework, FlexTry-On eliminates the need for scenario-specific architectures and maintains a consistent inference pipeline across different settings. Furthermore, the same framework supports multiple garment categories within a unified conditioning formulation, enabling a unified formulation across different virtual try-on scenarios. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FlexTry-On achieves competitive visual quality and strong FID [ 17 ] performance on both C2P and P2P benchmarks while maintaining efficient inference. In addition, the same framework can be directly applied to challenging cross-domain and in-the-wild scenarios. As shown in Fig. 2 , FlexTry-On achieves a favorable balance between synthesis quality, inference efficiency, and scenario flexibility, providing a practical step toward more flexible and widely applicable virtual try-on systems. Our contributions are summarized as: 1. We propose FlexTry-On, a unified and time-efficient diffusion-based framework that bridges cloth-to-person, person-to-person, cross-domain, and in-the-wild virtual try-on scenarios within a single framework. 2. We introduce a unified virtual try-on framework consisting of a Text-Aware Segmentation Module (TASM) and a Dual-DiT Tryon Module (DDTM), enabling conditioning from heterogeneous garment sources while jointly modeling garment appearance and person identity. We further employ a Style-GRAM loss for garment appearance preservation under noisy supervision. 3. Extensive evaluations on both standard benchmarks and challenging real-world settings demonstrate competitive visual quality, strong FID performance, and efficient inference within a unified framework. FlexTry-On supports all evaluated virtual try-on scenarios within a unified framework, as summarized in Tab. 1 . 2 Related Works IVTON [ 5 ] has evolved from warping-based pipelines to diffusion-based generative frameworks. Early methods [ 16 , 36 , 41 , 2 , 25 , 8 ] rely on explicit garment alignment and image synthesis, making them sensitive to pose variations, occlusions, and inaccurate geometric estimation. Recent diffusion-based approaches [ 49 , 32 , 13 , 22 , 3 , 45 , 4 , 23 , 15 , 26 , 29 ] significantly improve visual quality through large pre-trained models and attention-based mechanisms. Despite these advances, most existing methods are designed around specific conditioning assumptions. Many diffusion-based IVTON approaches assume a particular garment representation, such as clean product images, extracted garment regions, or reference-person-based garment cues, and design their conditioning mechanisms accordingly [ 49 , 32 , 13 , 22 , 3 , 45 , 4 , 23 , 15 , 26 , 29 ] . Consequently, their conditioning mechanisms are often tailored to specific input formats, limiting both flexibility and efficiency across different virtual try-on scenarios. Furthermore, most existing methods [ 49 , 32 , 13 , 22 , 3 , 45 , 4 , 23 , 26 , 29 ] implicitly assume category-consistent garment transfer, where the source and target garments belong to the same clothing category (e.g., upper-to-upper or dress-to-dress). Under this assumption, editable regions can be determined using predefined masks, human parsing labels, or garment extraction pipelines. However, transfers across different garment categories introduce ambiguous editable regions that cannot be uniquely determined using conventional category-based masking strategies. Recent methods, including Mask Does Not Matter [ 9 ] , All Parts Matter [ 10 ] , OmniTry [ 11 ] , OmniVTON [ 44 ] , and M&M VTO [ 48 ] , extend virtual try-on beyond the conventional cloth-to-person setting toward more diverse and realistic applications. Nevertheless, they are primarily designed for specific input assumptions and do not explicitly address category-crossing transfers. These observations suggest the key challenge is not only generating realistic try-on images but also designing a framework that can accommodate heterogeneous garment sources, identify task-aware editable regions, and support diverse virtual try-on scenarios without sacrificing inference efficiency. FlexTry-On consists of two key components: a Text-Aware Segmentation Module (TASM), which converts heterogeneous garment inputs into task-aware garment conditions and editable regions, and a Dual-DiT TryOn Module (DDTM), which synthesizes the final try-on image by jointly modeling garment appearance and person identity. For clarity, patchification and positional embeddings are omitted. 3.1 Text-Aware Segmentation Module (TASM) To support diverse virtual try-on scenarios, we introduce a Text-Aware Segmentation Module (TASM) that converts heterogeneous inputs into a unified conditioning representation. Unlike conventional human parsing models [ 28 ] or generic segmentation frameworks such as SAM [ 24 ] and Grounded-SAM [ 30 , 37 ] that are designed for pixel-level segmentation, TASM is designed specifically for virtual try-on conditioning and operates directly in the latent space. Given an image and predefined text conditions, TASM predicts garment-specific masks for downstream conditioning. As illustrated in Fig. 3 , TASM adopts a DiT-based architecture [ 35 ] and injects text conditions through multi-head cross-attention. Given a latent image representation, the module predicts region-specific masks corresponding to different garment categories. Specifically, only the predicted masks are retained for subsequent processing, while associated latent appearance features are discarded. An ablation of this design is provided in Appendix A.1 . However, the diffusion denoising objective primarily supervises image reconstruction and does not explicitly optimize garment fidelity, particularly on large-scale datasets with noisy garment-person correspondences [ 40 ] . Specifically, samples may share the same garment category while differing substantially in color, texture, or fine-grained appearance. Under such conditions, the model can satisfy the denoising objective while gradually reducing its reliance on garment-specific cues, leading to degraded garment fidelity. An illustrative mis-pairing example is provided in Fig. 5 . To bridge this gap, we introduce a GRAM-based Style Loss as a task-alignment constraint that explicitly encourages preservation of garment-specific appearance cues. Although GRAM-based style losses are not new [ 12 ] , our contribution lies in revisiting them as an optimization objective for virtual try-on rather than image stylization. Unlike pixel-wise reconstruction losses, which are incompatible with the geometric variations inherent in virtual try-on, the proposed loss operates on appearance statistics and remains invariant to spatial layout, making it particularly effective for preserving garment color and texture during synthesis. The style loss is defined as: ℒ s ​ t ​ y ​ l ​ e = MSE ⁡ ( G ⁡ ( z g ) , G ⁡ ( z o ​ u ​ t ⊙ M i ​ c ) ) , \mathcal{L}_{style}=\mathrm{MSE}\Big(G(z_{g}),\,G(z_{out}\odot M_{ic})\Big), (4) where G ⁡ ( ⋅ ) G(\cdot) denotes the Gram matrix, z g z_{g} represents the latent garment condition, and z o ​ u ​ t ⊙ M i ​ c z_{out}\odot M_{ic} extracts the predicted garment region from the denoised latent. This loss explicitly enforces the diffusion model to preserve garment-related appearance statistics throughout the synthesis process, ensuring that the generated output remains consistent with the reference garment in terms of color and texture. Unlike reconstruction-oriented objectives used in prior work [ 38 , 7 ] , the proposed GRAM-based loss does not aim to recover exact pixel values; instead, it serves as a task-aligned constraint that directly reflects the essential requirement of IVTON. As discussed in Sec. 4.3.2 , this design improves garment appearance preservation under both curated and noisy training, with substantially larger gains under noisy supervision, and helps maintain garment appearance under pose and identity variations. The total loss is formulated as: ℒ t ​ o ​ t ​ a ​ l = ℒ d ​ e ​ n ​ o ​ i ​ s ​ e + α s ​ t ​ y ​ l ​ e ​ ℒ s ​ t ​ y ​ l ​ e , \mathcal{L}_{total}=\mathcal{L}_{denoise}+\alpha_{style}\mathcal{L}_{style}, (5) where α s ​ t ​ y ​ l ​ e \alpha_{style} is the balance coefficient for the style loss. Publicly released checkpoints are used whenever available. For runtime evaluation, FlexTry-On uses 30 denoising steps, whereas each baseline follows its default inference configuration. All directly reproducible methods are measured with batch size 1 on a single RTX 4090 (24GB VRAM); exceptions and hardware normalization are detailed in Appendix E . All evaluations are conducted at 512 × 512 512\times 512 resolution. For methods without official implementations, we report paper-reported results. For OmniVTON [ 44 ] , we attempted to reproduce the official implementation but encountered unresolved issues and therefore retain its published quantitative results. FlexTry-On achieves the best paired/unpaired FID on both VITON-HD and DressCode-Upper among the evaluated methods while maintaining fast inference. Its efficiency comes from a single Reference-Net pass for garment feature extraction, followed by iterative denoising in the Main Net, avoiding repeated garment-side computation across denoising steps. Qualitative results in Fig. 7 further show more consistent garment texture and structure preservation, with fewer arm-region artifacts and clothing inconsistencies. 4.2.2 Full Dataset Training To support multiple IVTON scenarios within a single model, we train FlexTry-On* on the full combined C2P–P2P corpus. As shown in Tab. 1 , FlexTry-On* supports C2P, P2P, and cross-domain C2P/P2P, providing broader scenario coverage than the compared methods. We evaluate its standard C2P performance on the VITON-HD [ 2 ] and DressCode [ 33 ] Upper test sets. Compared with FlexTry-On trained only on VITON-HD and DressCode, FlexTry-On* shows a modest reduction in standard C2P performance (5.51/8.97 vs. 6.34/9.22 paired/unpaired FID on VITON-HD) , while enabling P2P and cross-domain scenarios within the same model. This illustrates the trade-off between optimizing for a single benchmark setting and supporting broader scenarios. As shown in Fig. 8 , FlexTry-On* supports P2P in both same-domain and zero-shot cross-domain settings. We further compare it with CatVTON and ITA-MDT*, a retrained variant of ITA-MDT. For cross-domain dress transfer, these methods require manually defined full-garment masks to specify the editable region because their original masking strategies are designed for category-consistent try-on. Even with these manually adapted masks, preserving garment structure and appearance across categories remains challenging. Meanwhile, TASM automatically constructs task-aware editable regions, allowing FlexTry-On* to produce more coherent results with better garment texture and structure preservation. Taken together, these controlled comparisons indicate that the observed gains cannot be explained by the broader training corpus alone, but also reflect the effectiveness of the proposed unified conditioning and generation framework. 5 Limitations FlexTry-On remains challenged by severe occlusion, unusual or oversized garments, and Street-to-Street cases involving uncontrolled pose, illumination, background, and occlusion. The current pipeline assumes a single selected visible person and does not automatically handle crowded or multi-person scenes. The combined training corpus may also inherit demographic and social-media biases. In addition, FlexTry-On does not consistently outperform all baselines on SSIM/LPIPS, despite achieving stronger FID in several settings. The OmniVTON comparison relies on paper-reported quantitative results because our local reproduction was unsuccessful. Additional discussion and failure analysis are provided in Appendices G and H . The full training corpus also contains weakly aligned garment–person pairs; ℒ s ​ t ​ y ​ l ​ e \mathcal{L}_{style} mitigates their effect on garment preservation but does not eliminate supervision noise. In practice, FlexTry-On targets single-person try-on applications where a target person and garment are specified before inference; automatic person selection in crowded scenes is outside the current scope. 6 Conclusion We present FlexTry-On, a unified framework for C2P, P2P, cross-domain, and in-the-wild virtual try-on. TASM provides task-aware editable regions, DDTM enables efficient synthesis with a single garment-reference pass, and ℒ s ​ t ​ y ​ l ​ e \mathcal{L}_{style} improves garment preservation under noisy supervision. FlexTry-On achieves competitive quality with 1.2-s inference, while matched retraining and qualitative results support its effectiveness across diverse try-on settings.
